title: Law Firms Want AI-Ready Lawyers: So Why Aren't They Hiring Them? — full episode transcript
pub: AI and the Future of Law / 2030 Vision, American Arbitration Association
author: Jen Leonard · Bridget McCormack

kp.k: Hiring signals undermine innovation in legal education
kp.d: Reporting Andy Perlman's panel remarks, McCormack and Leonard identify a mismatch between employers' expressed demand for practice readiness, interpersonal skills, judgment and technology competence and their continued reliance on school rankings, brands and Law Review. They argue that hiring for the desired competencies could reward innovative schools and induce wider curricular change; this is a proposed market mechanism, not an established hiring-outcomes finding.
qs: They are relying on rankings and brands even as they express frustration that they're not getting graduates with the skills that they're looking for.

If instead of thinking about a law school's ranking and Law Review and some of these traditional markers of quality in the hiring market, law firms could make a difference right away in how law schools think about what they're teaching and what they're training.

kp.k: Prospective students increasingly question preparation for technological change
kp.d: McCormack reports Perlman's observation that prospective Suffolk students are asking more sophisticated questions about training for a changed profession, including applicants who might not previously have considered a school outside the T14. She interprets applicant choice, alongside employers' hiring decisions, as a pressure point for educational reform. No applicant counts or systematic comparison are supplied.
qs: Prospective students are showing up at these kinds of events asking questions about what kind of training they're going to get to prepare them for a totally changed profession.
And he's seeing people show up at his events who might not have been there, you know, two years ago, four years ago, six years ago—because Suffolk Law School isn't in the T14.

kp.k: Future lawyer competencies emphasize human skills and legal foundations
kp.d: Leonard recounts Jordan Furlong's framework distinguishing knowledge, skills and ethics. His presentation portrayed document summaries, case analysis, memos and briefs as declining sources of distinctive lawyer value, favoring legal processes, reasoning and broad threshold concepts over first-year doctrinal depth, together with advocacy, negotiation, empathy and conflict resolution. This is a reported normative and predictive framework, not a measured account of task displacement.
qs: He had a slide that was basically the skills that we know lawyers to be valuable for historically (like drafting summaries of documents, analyzing case law, writing memos and briefs). And he just sort of had a big X across all of those.

And he talks about knowing legal processes and sources of law, understanding legal reasoning, and understanding threshold concepts in numerous legal areas versus a doctrinal deep dive into the topics we study as first years.
really thinks the future is about developing human skills that include advocating and negotiating, building relationships, displaying empathy, facilitating solutions, and resolving conflicts.

kp.k: Civil justice reform belongs within lawyers' ethical formation
kp.d: Leonard connects Furlong's ethics framework to defending the rule of law and repairing the civil justice system. She reports his criticism that the profession's failure in this area has contributed to undermining the rule of law. The discussion states an ethical priority rather than demonstrating an AI-driven access-to-justice outcome.
qs: something that I know that you and I focus on (and you have done amazing work around) is fixing the civil justice system so that we can fortify the rule of law.
We’ve really, Jordan said explicitly, dropped the ball as a profession there, which has led to a lot of the undermining of the rule of law.

kp.k: Legal audiences are shifting toward practical AI adoption
kp.d: Both hosts describe a perceived shift from skepticism to implementation over the preceding year, particularly from fall to spring. Leonard cites more solution-oriented audience questions and client surveys suggesting greater awareness and use, without providing survey methods, sample sizes or results. McCormack's Chicago and Riyadh audience experiences similarly offer anecdotal evidence of demand for faster change, while she acknowledges uneven readiness.
qs: And this spring, I have just noticed a huge jump in the sophistication of the questions—in the sort of solution-oriented nature of the questions.
How do we test things? How do we experiment without compromising data?
We run surveys with clients that also track this in attitudes and awareness—that people are much more aware and using this technology much more
I think people are still a little bit all over the map, but we’re definitely seeing more folks who are ready than even in the fall.

kp.k: AI-first deployment requires support for junior associates
kp.d: Leonard reports Nancy Green's approach at Miles & Stockbridge as encouraging AI experimentation across seniority levels and roles while giving junior associates room to learn. Leonard contrasts this with firms withholding information from nonpartners, which she argues increases anxiety about replacement. She presents possible job loss or insufficient thoughtfulness as alternative explanations, not documented causes.
qs: to try using AI first (this AI-first mindset) and see what you can do with it.
And she is also providing, I think, some cover for junior associates to really think about and learn the technology
I think a lot of firms are sort of hiding the ball from junior associates and others who are not partners. Which only elevates anxiety and makes people fearful of the technology.

kp.k: Mid-sized firms may compete through culture and adaptability
kp.d: Leonard argues that mid-sized firms can develop cohesive cultures and adapt nimbly under suitable leadership, whereas global firms' greater tool-testing resources do not necessarily translate into distinctiveness across large, mobile workforces. She reports Green's response to earlier on-campus interviewing: use it to build awareness among potential future mid-level lateral hires rather than pressure students into immediate commitments.
qs: Some of the big global law firms have the resources to test every tool imaginable, but across thousands of people who are moving all over the place, it's really hard to sustain culture or make your firm distinctive in any given way.

their response has been to not even view it as a place to hire law students (which I found really interesting), but a place to plant a seed that her firm is the place that maybe they want to come to as mid-level associates because they care about culture.

kp.k: Leadership renewal and transparency support organizational adaptation
kp.d: McCormack reports Green's planned departure from firm leadership to make room for new leaders, explicitly uncertain whether the horizon was one or two years. The hosts argue that transparent strategy and succession build trust during technological change, while retaining the value of experience. Leonard also recounts AAA staff moving from apprehension to competition over useful AI applications, based on interviews for an educational offering rather than quantified organizational research.
qs: There is a benefit, in the world we're living in where this technology is changing everything so quickly, to making room for new leaders.
They moved from this place of skepticism and fear and uncertainty around using AI to being competitive to find the best AI application and tool and resource.
I still believe transparency about what we're doing—what we're all doing—is as important to building trust and confidence as anything else.

kp.k: Human-plus-AI service remains the preferred professional analogy
kp.d: McCormack uses medicine to describe an augmentation model: AI performs analytical work while a professional who understands the individual explains options and supports decisions. She extends this potential to law. Leonard similarly anticipates legal and medical work shifting toward empathy and decision support, suggesting the professions could learn from each other's educational responses; these are analogies and expectations rather than comparative evidence.
qs: Like, I really want my radiologist to have AI read my scans—and then I want to talk to her about what they show.

I want the human who knows me, knows my family, knows my priorities and what I care about—to talk with me about whether we’re just waiting three months for another scan or doing something more aggressive.
And there’s no reason why that shouldn’t be true in law too. We can be better with this technology.
maybe professions like law and medicine are moving in similar directions and can learn from one another how to teach better.

kp.k: Routine research is portrayed as dramatically faster
kp.d: Leonard contrasts weeks spent preparing 50-state surveys as a summer associate with her expectation that Deep Research could complete one in under two minutes. Together with her comments on document summarization, this illustrates the hosts' expectation of major task compression. The transcript supplies no timed test, quality assessment or account of human verification for the survey claim.
qs: I remember doing 50-state surveys as a summer and it took weeks, an unbelievable amount of time, to review the law of 50 states.
Deep Research can do that in under two minutes now, I'm sure.

kp.k: Natural-language building lowers barriers but exposes data limitations
kp.d: McCormack describes generating a memo diagram through AI-written code without coding training; Leonard describes Claude producing a capacity-planning dashboard for her business. Leonard notes that all numbers beyond those she supplied were made up and anticipates improved usefulness after correcting assumptions. They speculate that increasingly capable agentic systems could integrate data sources and challenge standalone software business models; no functioning integration or market impact is demonstrated.
qs: it produced this beautiful diagram that was exactly how my brain was visualizing it.
The only issue was that all of the numbers were made up, except for the ones I provided in the prompt.

If we are all just able to, especially as agentic systems become more sophisticated and AI can go off and access different places and come back and use that to populate something in an LLM, what does that mean for the business model of software?

kp.k: Model advances promise simpler interfaces and broader applications
kp.d: McCormack reports Google's co-scientist as a multi-agent research system she has not tested and Claude 3.7 Sonnet as automatically shifting between quick answers and deliberative problem solving. The hosts welcome reduced model-selection burdens. McCormack anticipates a similarly unified GPT-5 by spring but explicitly frames that timing and functionality as her interpretation, not established delivery.
qs: It's a multi-agent system built to help researchers with hypothesis generation and experiments, in service of better science and faster scientific discoveries
You can ask simple questions or complex questions, and you don't have to switch between models—something you still have to do with OpenAI.
I don't know exactly what that means, but it sounds like by spring sometime we're going to get that model that combines all the capabilities into one place.

kp.k: Court replacement appears as a reported vendor ambition
kp.d: McCormack reports xAI advertising Grok 3 as a direct, fast and free destination for legal questions and disputes that could displace courts. She treats this as a signal that the technology company targets legal services, while expressly doubting imminent court replacement. The transcript does not establish adjudicative authority, deployment or performance.
qs: one of the things that xAI advertised when it was released was that it was going to displace courts, that you could take all of your legal questions and legal disputes directly to Grok 3 and it would handle it for you in no time and for no money.
I don't think that Grok 3 is going to replace courts tomorrow, but it was a pretty interesting signal that at least xAI views the legal profession as a target.

kp.k: Near-term AGI discussion raises preparedness questions, not findings
kp.d: The hosts report technology-sector conversations suggesting AGI might arrive later in 2025 or in the following year, while Leonard acknowledges contested definitions. Drawing on interviews with Dario Amodei and Ezra Klein's interview with Ben Buchanan, she argues that public discussion inadequately addresses practical social and employment consequences. Her comparison of Claude and ChatGPT preparation advice illustrates differing generated tones, not validated forecasts or established preparation strategies.
qs: In fact, you hear people say maybe even later this year, and if not that, then probably next year, that we will have artificial general intelligence.
I think there are all different kinds of definitions as to what this is and when we'll know that we're there.

I think Ezra Klein's position was that we're just not at all prepared or really having sufficiently sophisticated and creative conversations beyond “there will be job loss and we'll have universal basic income” or “jobs will be lost and new ones will be created—that's what always happens.”
I don't know that I have any really concrete ideas—other than investing in AI-related industries—that come out of those things.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Leonard claims AI can take over document summarization and dramatically accelerate multijurisdictional legal research.
pts.d: Jen Leonard treats manual document summarization as an activity that AI has already made unnecessary in her experience. She also predicts, with expressed confidence rather than a reported test, that Deep Research can complete a 50-state survey in under two minutes, compared with the weeks she remembers spending on such assignments.

pts.k: Furlong's framework anticipates a shift from document production and analysis toward human, practical and ethical competencies.
pts.d: As reported by Leonard, Jordan Furlong crossed out historically valuable activities such as drafting summaries, analyzing case law and writing memos and briefs, then emphasized legal processes, sources, reasoning, threshold knowledge across legal areas, human skills and professional ethics. This is Furlong's proposed framework, conveyed secondhand, not a directly interviewed statement or an observed occupational outcome.

pts.k: McCormack presents human-plus-AI service delivery as an opportunity to improve law rather than simply replace lawyers.
pts.d: Bridget McCormack uses a medical analogy: AI performs technical analysis while a trusted professional helps a person interpret the result and make decisions. She extends that augmentation model to law. Leonard similarly envisages professionals spending more time helping people make decisions. McCormack separately maintains that human experience remains valuable and is not replaceable by ChatGPT.

pts.k: Perlman's reported argument is that hiring incentives, not stated employer preferences alone, determine whether legal education rewards AI-ready competencies.
pts.d: Andy Perlman, as recounted by McCormack, argues that employers could rapidly change law-school behavior by recruiting for future-relevant skills instead of school ranking and Law Review credentials. Leonard interprets the current problem as a mismatch between employers' requests for practice-ready, technologically capable graduates and their continued reliance on prestige. She predicts that changed hiring criteria would spread innovative education beyond Suffolk.

pts.k: Perlman reports emerging student demand for education suited to a changed legal profession.
pts.d: As recounted by McCormack, Perlman says prospective Suffolk students increasingly ask about preparation for technological change, and some applicants who previously might have prioritized more highly ranked schools are now attending Suffolk events. McCormack interprets prospective students as another source of pressure on law schools to change. The account does not establish a market-wide shift in enrollment.

pts.k: Leonard and McCormack report a recent transition from skepticism toward practical experimentation among legal audiences.
pts.d: Leonard describes increasingly sophisticated questions about testing AI and protecting data, alongside greater awareness and use in client surveys. McCormack reports similar changes in conference audiences and arbitration discussions. Both describe adoption readiness as increasing, while McCormack explicitly says that readiness remains uneven.

pts.k: Leonard and McCormack identify leadership, transparency and organizational culture as important to AI adoption.
pts.d: Leonard reports Nancy Green's AI-first deployment strategy at Miles & Stockbridge and her support for junior associates learning the technology. Leonard argues that withholding information can increase employees' anxiety and that mid-sized firms can have cultural and adaptability advantages over global firms, despite the latter's greater resources. McCormack argues that technology is already capable of much of the desired work but people still need support. Leonard reports that AAA staff moved from fear toward competition to identify useful applications. Green's reported decision to make room for new leadership is presented as another adaptation to rapid change.

pts.k: The episode distinguishes an advertised court-substitution ambition from a conditional opportunity for ADR providers.
pts.d: McCormack reports that xAI advertised Grok 3 as capable of handling legal questions and disputes quickly and without cost, displacing courts. This is attributed to xAI, not adopted as McCormack's forecast; she doubts immediate court replacement and treats the advertisement as a signal of legal-market targeting. Separately, McCormack suggests ADR providers could gain advantages by adapting AI to cross-border dispute resolution.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Task-transformation claims rely on personal experience and illustrative reasoning, not demonstrated legal-work benchmarks.
pts.d: Leonard supplies firsthand recollections of manual research and experience using AI, but does not report testing a 50-state survey or checking its completeness and accuracy. Her under-two-minute estimate is explicitly an expression of confidence. Furlong's future-skills framework is supported through a reported conference presentation. McCormack's human-plus-AI argument is a service-user analogy rather than evidence of measured improvements in legal outcomes.

pts.k: Claims about adoption and education draw on qualitative observations, unspecified client surveys and secondhand leadership accounts.
pts.d: Leonard cites surveys without sample sizes, field dates, methods or numerical results, alongside her experience presenting to law firms. McCormack cites audience reactions and conversations, including in Riyadh. Perlman's account of prospective students and Green's firm strategy are reported from the panel, rather than supported by admissions or hiring statistics. AAA staff interviews supply an organizational example of changing attitudes, not a quantified causal finding about transparency.

pts.k: Court substitution is presented as vendor advertising, while ADR advantages are a conditional proposition.
pts.d: The transcript supplies no legal dispute-resolution trial, case outcome or legal-specific benchmark supporting xAI's reported advertisement. McCormack mentions Grok 3's general benchmark performance without naming tests or reporting scores; this is not evidence of court-replacement capability. Her ADR proposition is based on her professional discussion of potential applications, without measured results.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Routine-task capability is described as current; wider professional restructuring has no fixed deadline.
pts.d: In this 2025 episode, Leonard characterizes summarization displacement and very rapid research as present possibilities. Furlong's skills framework and the hosts' proposed shift toward human-centered work concern the future without a dated transition. McCormack's preferred model currently retains a trusted human, while allowing that direct interaction with AI might become acceptable later. The claims do not specify requirements for human verification of legal research.

pts.k: The observed attitude shift is recent, and education reform is conditional on changed purchasing and hiring behavior.
pts.d: Leonard locates the change in legal audiences between the preceding fall and the current spring, describing a six-to-twelve-month period. Perlman's reported claim that employers could change education 'tomorrow' or 'right away' conveys potential speed, not a scheduled reform. Scaling the Suffolk approach depends on employers actually rewarding competencies instead of prestige and students valuing corresponding educational returns.

pts.k: Organizational advantages and dispute-resolution changes are qualified rather than unconditional forecasts.
pts.d: Leonard conditions mid-sized firms' adaptability on size and leadership. McCormack conditions ADR advantages on successful adaptation of AI and expressly doubts court replacement 'tomorrow.' Green's succession plan is recalled uncertainly as one or two years away. Although the episode discusses industry expectations of AGI in 2025 or 2026, it does not establish those expectations as a demonstrated capability or attach a precise legal-market transition date to them.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Law students, junior lawyers, law schools and legal employers face changing skill requirements and selection incentives.
pts.d: Students and associates are the clearest examples of people whose traditional research and summarization tasks may change. Law schools face pressure to teach technology use, practical competencies and human skills. Prospective students can influence educational demand; law firms, as purchasers of talent, can reward those competencies through hiring. Leonard identifies opportunities for innovative schools and professional-development leaders, without quantifying graduate employment effects.

pts.k: Mid-sized and global law firms face different organizational opportunities, while employees across seniority levels face adoption pressures.
pts.d: Leonard contrasts mid-sized firms' potential cultural cohesion and agility with global firms' greater resources and difficulty sustaining distinctiveness across large, mobile workforces. Green's reported AI-first strategy includes senior partners, junior associates and other roles. Lack of transparency may intensify junior employees' fear of dismissal, but the episode supplies no measured layoffs or firm-wide staffing forecast. Leadership renewal is proposed as helpful while experienced professionals retain value.

pts.k: Clients, disputants, courts and ADR providers could encounter different delivery models.
pts.d: The human-plus-AI model would let clients receive technologically assisted analysis alongside relationship-based human guidance. xAI's reported ambition instead implies direct reliance on AI for legal questions and disputes, potentially substituting for courts. McCormack's separate proposition concerns ADR providers competing through AI-enabled cross-border dispute-resolution services. These remain distinct models; the transcript does not document improved access-to-justice outcomes or actual court displacement.
